newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French shares plunge on poll rumours.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French shares plunge on poll rumours.

text.p: French stocks plunged on Wednesday on rumours of private opinion polls which traders said showed the left well placed for the second round of the parliamentary election on Sunday.
But the bond market, which analysts said had priced in much earlier the chances of a Socialist victory in the election, was only slightly weaker, while the franc was steady.

The CAC-40 share index fell 4.44 percent to a low of 2,561.23 shortly after the poll rumours hit, exceeding the 3.9 percent drop on Monday after the first round of voting put the combined left ahead of the ruling centre-right coalition.
Monday's fall was the biggest drop in four years.
Analysts said the stock market feared a Socialist-led government would make it harder for private companies to lay off staff and slow down France's privatisation programme.
"Indications that the left could win the election are the catalyst for the share fall," said Gary Dugan, market strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"There are significant market concerns over the prospect of the Socialists winning the election," Mike Young, director of European investment strategy at Goldman Sachs in London.
"I think we've seen the extent of today's fall," a trader said, adding that the market was being bombarded by rumours and was feeling fragile with more private polls expected.
Analysts said the CAC-40 index could fall to 2,450-2,500 points if the left won on Sunday.
In the bond market, though, the spread between French 10-year government bonds and equivalent German bunds, a key barometer of market confidence in France, was little changed.
French bonds (OATs) were yielding nine basis points less than German bunds, compared to 10 on Monday.
Market analysts have said they believe a Socialist-led government would not affect France's commitment to launching a single European currency in 1999.
"What's the real difference between the left and the right? It's six of one, half a dozen of the other," a head of a French brokerage said.

Caroline Newhouse Cohen at Louis Dreyfus in Paris said that if National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, tipped as a possible prime minister if the centre wins, had similar views on the need for Europe to focus on jobs and growth as Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin.

One market operator also noted that the better the Socialist showing was on Sunday, the less dependent it would be on support from the Communist party, which has said it wants a new referendum on monetary union.
The Socialist party would need 289 seats to have an absolute majority in parliament.
A televised speech by President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday night, in which he warned French people of the danger of returning to Socialism, failed to impress the market.
French law forbids the publication of opinion polls from one week before the first round of voting. Published polls before the news blackout showed the centre-right in the lead.
